propositions.text: This is an appeal of a July 7, 2016 decision by a Citizenship Judge refusing the Applicant's citizenship application.
propositions.quote: This is an appeal of a decision dated July 7, 2016, rendered by a Citizenship Judge refusing the Applicant’s application for citizenship on the ground that the Applicant failed to meet the requirements of paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Citizenship Act, RSC 1985, c C-29 [Act].

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is an appeal of a July 7, 2016 Citizenship Judge decision refusing the Applicant's citizenship application.

propositions.text: Applicant is a 31-year-old Iranian citizen who arrived in Canada July 13, 2008 and became a permanent resident.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, aged 31, is a citizen of Iran. He arrived in Canada on July 13, 2008 and became a permanent resident.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for citizenship August 28, 2013; reference period for residency is August 28, 2009 to August 28, 2013.
propositions.quote: He applied for citizenship on August 28, 2013. Therefore, the reference period for the purposes of determining residency in accordance with the law spans from August 28, 2009 to August 28, 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a 31-year-old Iranian citizen who became a permanent resident in 2008 and applied for citizenship in 2013, defining the residency reference period.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge refused Applicant's citizenship application for not meeting residency requirement under paragraph 5(1)(c).
propositions.quote: On July 7, 2016, the Citizenship Judge refused the Applicant’s application for citizenship on the basis that the Applicant did not meet the residency requirement under paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Act.

propositions.text: Applicant demonstrated 1039 days physical presence, 421 days absence, shortfall of 56 days from 1095 days required.
propositions.quote: The Citizenship Judge found that the Applicant had demonstrated 1039 days of physical presence, 421 days of absence, and a shortfall of 56 days from 1095 days required by the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The Citizenship Judge found the Applicant had 1039 days physical presence, 421 days absence, and refused citizenship for 56-day shortfall under paragraph 5(1)(c).

propositions.text: Applying Pourghasemi test, Citizenship Judge concluded Applicant did not provide sufficient credible evidence of 1095 days physical presence.
propositions.quote: Applying the test of Re: Pourghasemi, [1993] FCJ No 232 [Pourghasemi], the Citizenship Judge concluded that the Applicant did not provide sufficient and credible evidence to establish his physical presence in Canada for a minimum of 1095 days during the reference period.

propositions.text: Judge found discrepancies in Applicant's work and study history between application and residence questionnaire.
propositions.quote: She found that there were discrepancies in the Applicant’s work and study history between his application and residence questionnaire.

paragraphs.summary: The Citizenship Judge applied Pourghasemi test and found insufficient credible evidence and discrepancies in Applicant's work and study history.

propositions.text: Did the Citizenship Judge err in finding Applicant did not meet residence requirements?
propositions.quote: This matter raises the following issues: 1) Did the Citizenship Judge err in finding that the Applicant did not meet the residence requirements of the law?

propositions.text: Did the Citizenship Judge err by not raising concerns about Applicant's credibility at hearing?
propositions.quote: 2) Did the Citizenship Judge err by not raising concerns with the Applicant’s credibility at the hearing?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies two issues: whether the Citizenship Judge erred on residence requirements and on raising credibility concerns.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge's findings on residence requirements are mixed fact and law, reviewed on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: A Citizenship Judge’s findings on the fulfilment of the residence requirements as dictated by paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Act is a question of mixed fact and law which should be reviewed on the standard of reasonableness.

propositions.text: Decision must be justified, transparent, intelligible, and within a range of acceptable outcomes (Dunsmuir).
propositions.quote: The decision must be justified, transparent, and intelligible, and must fall within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes defensible in respect of the facts and law (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47 [Dunsmuir]).

paragraphs.summary: The court states that findings on residence requirements are mixed fact and law reviewed for reasonableness, citing Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness questions reviewed on correctness standard (Khosa).
propositions.quote: Whether the Applicant had the opportunity to address the Citizenship Judge’s concerns about his credibility raises a question of procedural fairness which should be reviewed on the standard of correctness (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] 1 SCR 339).

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness questions are reviewed on correctness standard, citing Khosa.

propositions.text: Paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Act requires permanent residents to have at least three years residence in Canada within four years before application.
propositions.quote: At the time of the Applicant’s application for citizenship, paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Act prescribed following residence requirements read as follows: ... has, within the four years immediately preceding the date of his or her application, accumulated at least three years of residence in Canada ...

propositions.text: Residence is calculated as one day per day after lawful admission, half day per day before lawful admission.
propositions.quote: (i) for every day during which the person was resident in Canada before his lawful admission to Canada for permanent residence the person shall be deemed to have accumulated one-half of a day of residence, and (ii) for every day during which the person was resident in Canada after his lawful admission to Canada for permanent residence the person shall be deemed to have accumulated one day of residence;

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal residence requirements under paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Act and how residence days are calculated.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge erred by not assessing establishment in Canada as threshold question despite documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The Applicant claims that the Citizenship Judge erred in failing to assess the Applicant’s establishment in Canada as a threshold question, although he submitted documentary evidence of his establishment of residence (Hao v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 46).

propositions.text: Decision is unreasonable because Judge ignored relevant evidence of physical presence during reference period.
propositions.quote: The Applicant further argues that the decision is unreasonable because the Citizenship Judge ignored relevant evidence demonstrating his physical presence in Canada during the relevant period of reference (Dhaliwal v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2015 FC 157 at paras 85-86).

propositions.text: Judge breached procedural fairness by not informing Applicant of concerns about missing transcripts and speculating on online courses.
propositions.quote: Finally, the Applicant asserts that the Citizenship Judge breached her duty of procedural fairness by failing to inform the Applicant at the hearing of her concerns regarding the lack of transcripts from the University of Reading and from the University of Ottawa, and by rather speculating on whether the Applicant had taken courses for his degrees online or by distance learning.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Judge erred by not assessing establishment, ignoring evidence, and breaching procedural fairness about missing transcripts.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge's threshold residency determination can be presumed (Boland).
propositions.quote: The Respondent contends that the Citizenship Judge’s assessment of the threshold residency determination can be presumed (Boland v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 376 [Boland].

propositions.text: Decision was reasonable; Judge properly applied Pourghasemi test and found insufficient credible evidence of physical presence.
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the decision was reasonable; the Citizenship Judge properly applied the Pourghasemi test and reasonably concluded that the Applicant failed to provide sufficient credible evidence establishing his physical presence in Canada during the reference period for his application.

propositions.text: Judge did not ignore evidence but weighed it and found it insufficient.
propositions.quote: She did not ignore documentary evidence provided by the Applicant in support of his presence in Canada, but rather weighed this evidence and found it insufficient.

propositions.text: Disputes procedural fairness breach; Judge had no duty to request additional documents and Applicant had opportunity to address inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: Lastly, the Respondent disputes the alleged procedural fairness breach, underlining that the Citizenship Judge had no duty to request specific additional documents (Zheng v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 1311) and that the Applicant was given the opportunity to address inconsistencies in the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Judge's threshold residency finding can be presumed, decision was reasonable, evidence was weighed, and no procedural fairness breach occurred.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge did not err in rejecting Applicant's citizenship application or breach procedural fairness by omitting to request additional evidence.
propositions.quote: The Court determines that the Citizenship Judge neither committed a reviewable error in rejecting the Applicant’s citizenship application by determining that his physical presence in Canada was not established nor a breach of procedural fairness by omitting to request additional documentary evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Citizenship Judge did not err or breach procedural fairness in rejecting the application or omitting to request more evidence.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge's threshold residency determination may be implicit or presumed (Boland).
propositions.quote: As stated by the Respondent, it is trite law that, in assessing residence requirements under paragraph 5(1)(c) of the Act following the two-part approach established by our Court’s jurisprudence, a Citizenship Judge’s threshold residency determination ought not to be explicit, but may be presumed or implicit in the Citizenship Judge’s reasons: [22] … it must be presumed that the Citizenship Judge was prepared to accept that the Applicant had established residence on the day of landing, otherwise there would have been no reason to determine whether the Applicant’s residency satisfied the statutorily prescribed number of days. That being the case, I fail to understand what the Applicant is complaining about, as the Citizenship Judge implicitly decided that he had satisfied the first part of the analysis and had established residency at the earliest possible date. (Boland, above, at para 22)

paragraphs.summary: The court states that the Citizenship Judge's threshold residency determination may be implicit or presumed, citing Boland.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge's threshold residency determination was implicit.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the Citizenship Judge’s threshold residency determination was implicit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Citizenship Judge's threshold residency determination was implicit.

propositions.text: Applicant bears onus to provide sufficient evidence of residency compliance.
propositions.quote: The Court notes that the Applicant bears the onus of providing sufficient evidence demonstrating his compliance with the residency requirements of the law.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge found many inconsistencies and discrepancies in Applicant's evidence, including study dates and documents.
propositions.quote: In her decision, the Citizenship Judge raised many inconsistencies and discrepancies in the evidence submitted by the Applicant; the dates of his studies at the Allameh Tabatabaei University (Iran), at the University of Reading (United Kingdom) and at the University of Ottawa were incomplete and inconsistent, and there were discrepancies in some of the documentary evidence, such as the translation of his Iranian Bachelor’s degree and his Aeroplan Activity Report.

propositions.text: Decision was reasonable; Judge could weigh evidence and conclude physical presence requirements not met.
propositions.quote: In light of these shortcomings, the decision was reasonable, as it was open to the Citizenship Judge to weigh the evidence and to conclude that the physical presence requirements were not met by the Applicant (Reference is made to paragraph 16 and, also, paragraph 26 to 30 inclusive of the judgment in Fotros v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 842 [Fotros], penned by Justice Simon Fothergill; and, also, paragraph 25 to 27 inclusive of the judgment in Ballout v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 978, penned by Justice Marie-Josée Bédard).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant bears the onus, the Judge found inconsistencies, and the decision was reasonable to deny citizenship.

propositions.text: Citizenship Judge met duty of procedural fairness; Applicant not entitled to specific additional document requests.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the Court finds that the Citizenship Judge’s duty of procedural fairness was met. The Applicant was not entitled to specific, additional document requests in order to complete his file (Fotros, above, at para 11).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Citizenship Judge met procedural fairness and Applicant was not entitled to additional document requests.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed; no serious question of general importance to certify.
propositions.quote: The appeal is dismissed. JUDGMENT THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the appeal be dismissed. There is no serious question of general importance to be certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and declines to certify a serious question of general importance.
